narration: There is a city with no people in it. And your photos live there.

narration: Where your photos actually live.
You take a photo. The app says it is safe in the cloud.
The cloud is not in the sky. It is a building full of computers.
note: The myth is named out loud before it is corrected

narration: Thousands of machines, stacked in racks, in a warehouse with no windows.
Every one of them needs power, and every search turns into heat.
First your photo is copied. Then it is checked. Then it is stored, more than once.
note: Three steps: count-three matches

narration: Good storage keeps copies in separate buildings, so one flood cannot erase your holiday.
All of it adds up to about one and a half percent of the world's electricity.
note: Sourced: IEA via Our World in Data

narration: It is not magic. It is a building, a power bill, and a very patient security guard.
Copied. Checked. Stored. Powered.

narration: So when you hit back up, you know exactly where it goes.

narration: You did not get replaced by AI. You got replaced by a checklist.
How AI automation actually works.
Automation just means steps a machine follows without asking you first.
For fifty years those steps were rules. If this, then that.
note: Rules only. No thinking. Short sentence, big point.

narration: Rules break the moment real life looks slightly different from the example.
Now add a model. Something that reads a messy pile and guesses the sensible thing.
note: Analogy: a very well-read assistant who never says I do not know unless you make them

narration: Set a goal. Give it tools. Check the result. Go again.

note: Four steps is the payload of the whole episode

narration: That loop is the automation. The model is only one part of it.
It is not one genius robot. It is a loop with a safety check bolted on.
And the check is where it fails. No check means no automation, just vibes.
Goal. Tools. Check. Repeat.
So next time someone says the AI does it, ask where the check is.
Nothing on the internet is free. But some free things are genuinely worth it.
How to tell if a free tool is actually free.
Every free thing is paid for somehow. There are only four ways.
You pay with attention. Or with data. Or later. Or somebody else pays.
note: Four chips: this is the saveable frame

narration: Ads mean the product is your attention. The tool is just the delivery.
Data means the tool learns you, and that is the actual price of entry.
And later means the free tier runs out exactly when you are hooked.
Somebody else means a community, a school, or an open source project pays.
So ask one question before you sign up. If I never pay, who is paying for this?

note: The one line a viewer can reuse

narration: Free and private is rare and worth finding. Free and mining you is everywhere.

narration: Attention. Data. Later. Somebody else.
Ask who pays. Then enjoy the free stuff without the uneasy feeling.

narration: Your wifi does not hate you. It has rush hour.
Why your wifi dies at nine pm.
Wifi is radio. It travels through the same air as everyone else's.
On the crowded band there are only three channels that do not overlap.
note: Sourced: 2.4 GHz has channels 1, 6, 11

narration: So your neighbours' routers are already talking over yours.
At nine, everyone in the building starts streaming at the same time.
And the internet coming into your home is shared with your street, not just your flat.

narration: It is not your provider being evil. It is a queue, and queues have a shape.
Shared air. Shared pipe. Everyone at once.
Try the cable tonight. You will hear the difference in one video.
You posted one photo. Seconds later there were copies you will never see.
What actually happens when you post.
Your phone sends it up. The app immediately makes several smaller versions.
Those copies sit on servers in many cities, near the people who will view them.
And every viewer's phone keeps its own copy, quietly, to load it faster.
A screenshot is also a copy. The app cannot delete it, ever.
Deleting removes your copy and the public link. Not the screenshots.
The photo can also carry hidden data: where it was taken, when, and on what.
note: EXIF metadata

narration: Three habits. Strip the location. Share to a small group first. Assume it is permanent.

narration: None of this is a reason to stop posting. It is a reason to post on purpose.
note: The line that keeps the episode from being fear-mongering

narration: Copies. Caches. Screenshots. Metadata.
Post like it is permanent. Because the internet already does.
An AI that answers your question and an AI that actually does the task? They are not quite the same thing.
note: Cold open on two panels: a bubble and a task list.

narration: Think of a chatbot as someone you can ask for directions. You ask, it explains the route.
An AI agent is closer to an assistant that can use tools.
You might ask it to find a meeting time. It could check an available calendar, compare slots, and prepare an invitation.
The difference is not that one is magically intelligent. It is what the system is set up to do.
A chatbot usually gives you a response. An agent can work through steps: plan, use a tool, check the result, then continue.
But here is the catch: agents can make mistakes, misunderstand a goal, or take an action you did not intend.
note: The caveat is its own beat so the card can be read at full size.

narration: Important actions should have clear permissions and human approval.
A chatbot responds. An agent can take steps.
note: The two columns read out loud; the thesis line is saved for the sign-off.

narration: So remember: answers are one thing; taking steps are another.
note: Finger heart, takeaway and disclosure visible. The thesis line lands here, not on the recap.

narration: Cloudflare and Docker both show up in web projects.

narration: Treating them as alternatives is like comparing a road network with a shipping box.
note: The analogy is the beat, so it gets four angles: both, the map, the route on the map, then the box. The ring changes hands on the word.

narration: Docker packs an app with the pieces it needs: code, libraries, settings.
note: A box on the bench and three named pieces going into it, one per noun in the sentence.

narration: That package is an image. Run it, and it becomes a container.
note: The same box twice, with a play control between them: the only difference between an image and a container is whether it is running.

narration: Cloudflare does a different job: it sits in front of your site.
note: Visitors on the left, the site on the right, and the layer that stands between them drawn in on the word "front".

narration: It can route visitors, keep copies of pages near them, and block bad traffic.
note: Three jobs on one bench: the short route, a copy of the page beside each visitor, and a parcel stopped at the shield.

narration: A team builds the app in Docker, runs it on a server, and puts Cloudflare in front.
note: The whole stack assembles in the order the sentence says it: box, server, then the layer in front.

narration: Two layers, two jobs. The app is packed, the traffic is handled.
note: Two cards, stacked rather than opposed: this is the beat where the pair stops looking like a choice.

narration: They are not competitors. Each does what the other does not.
note: The same two cards side by side with the difference marked between them: the comparison is the point, so the ring moves across both.

narration: Cloudflare doesn't host your app. Docker doesn't secure it.
note: Each card loses the thing people assume it does, and the cat holds the cards up while both claims are crossed out.

narration: Docker packages the app. Cloudflare delivers and protects it.
note: The recap is the two job cards again, unchanged, because nothing about them changed - only what the viewer can now read on them.

narration: Different jobs. Sometimes, one stack.
